question: The resignation of Harvard President Claudine Gay in January 2024 following accusations of antisemitism and plagiarism highlighted the failure of the policy of positive discrimination. A political activist heading up the world’s most prestigious university, Gay had less impact on the academic world through her work (plagiarised) than by her trivialisation of acts of antisemitism.

This is an extremely serious precedent and one that must be strongly condemned to ensure it does happen again under any circumstances. It is just one of many cases that have been reported and is sure to raise concerns about the situation on American and European campuses. 1.
Does the Commission intend to continue to advocate positive discrimination, which has been used here to appoint and cover up an antisemitic activist?

Will the European Commission, which defends the concept of academic freedom, impose strict criteria in universities hosting Erasmus students to protect them from the harmful consequences of such woke ideas?
answer: The EU committed to address all forms of antisemitism in line with the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as indicated in the 2021 EU Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (1).

Following the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023, the Commission is accelerating the implementation of this strategy in line with the communication ‘No Place for Hate: A Europe united against hatred’ (2). According to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (3), Member States are fully responsible for the organisation of their education systems and for the content of teaching.

In the EU, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (4) includes the freedom of expression and information, as well as the freedom of the arts and sciences specifying that academic freedom shall be respected. However, the provisions of the Charter are binding for the Member States when they are implementing EU law.

Nonetheless, the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education (ECHE) (5) specifies that participating institutions in the Erasmus+ programme must respect in full the principles of non-discrimination, transparency and inclusion and ensure that students are aware of their rights and obligations as defined in the Erasmus Student Charter (6).

The latter specifies that students are entitled to academic freedom in communicating or sharing ideas and facts. Commitment to the principles of the ECHE is the prerequisite for universities to participate in the Erasmus+ Programme, and their implementation is monitored by the Erasmus+ national agencies.
